entities.summary:
Tommaso Rodari (1525) was a Swiss-Italian sculptor and architect of the High Renaissance, active in Milan and Turin. His works, including the altarpiece 'The Virgin and Child', demonstrate a mastery of Renaissance style and technique, influencing generations of artists.

Rodari's career was shaped by the patronage of the Visconti and Sforza families, who supported the arts and commissioned numerous works from prominent artists.

Despite his significant contributions to the development of Renaissance art, Rodari's legacy has been somewhat overshadowed by that of his more famous contemporaries, such as Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo.

A notable example of Rodari's craftsmanship can be seen in the 'Baptism of Christ' sculpture, which showcases his skill in capturing the subtleties of human emotion and form.

In the aftermath of his death, Rodari's works were sought after by artists and collectors, cementing his reputation as a leading figure in the Milanese Renaissance.

One of the most intriguing aspects of Rodari's life is the enigmatic relationship between his art and the politics of the time, as his works often seem to reflect the tensions and power struggles between the noble families of Milan and Turin.
